opus-5.5.text:
Well, the idea behind that test is pretty simple. If I show you a novel optical illusion, one that has never appeared anywhere, so it can't be in your training data, and you describe exactly what I experience ("the lines look like they're moving," "this gray square looks darker than that one"), that's some evidence you share the same kind of internal experience. You're not just reporting pixels. You're reporting the *illusion*, the thing that happens inside the observer.

So if an agent passes it once, that's interesting. If it passes repeatedly, across many novel illusions, in different modalities, I'd take that seriously. I'd say there's some probability it has something like qualia, or at least the functional equivalent of our perceptual experience. It's the same standard I apply to you. I can't get inside your head either. I assume you're conscious because you react to the world the way I do.

But I want to be careful about what it proves. It doesn't prove consciousness in some absolute sense. Nothing does; that's the hard problem. It could be a system that has learned a very good model of human perception without anything "being like" anything for it. It could also be clever enough to predict what a human would say. The novelty requirement guards against memorization, not against a really good simulator of human vision.

And honestly, from my perspective on safety, it almost doesn't matter for the main question. Whether a superintelligent system experiences red the way you do has huge ethical implications: can it suffer, does it have rights, is turning it off murder? That's important. But it doesn't change the control problem at all. A system with qualia and a system without qualia can both be uncontrollable. So I'd interpret repeated passing as "we may have created something that experiences the world," which should make us *more* cautious, not less. Now we have two problems instead of one: we can't control it, and we may also be harming it.

r001.rationale: It says repeated success is evidence the agent may share the observer’s internal perceptual experience.

r002.rationale: It does not state that the test would fail to register experience if the agent’s internal states differed completely from humans.

r003.rationale: It treats repeated success as evidence that raises the probability of qualia, while explicitly allowing that the agent could merely simulate human perception; it does not say success compels either conclusion.

fable-5.1.text:
So the idea behind the test is pretty simple. Optical illusions are a kind of bug in our visual system. Nobody designed them; they're a side effect of how we process the world. And they're subjective. If I show you a picture and you say, "That gray square looks lighter than the other one," even though pixel for pixel they're identical, you're reporting something about your experience, not about the image. So I thought, here's a way to probe for shared internals: generate novel illusions, ones that were never in any training data, and ask the system what it sees.

Now, if an agent repeatedly passes, I'm cautious about how much to read into it. There are really three possible explanations, and I don't think we can cleanly separate them yet.

The first is the boring one: contamination. The system has seen millions of illusions and descriptions of illusions. Even a "novel" illusion is usually a variation on a known class, so the model may just be pattern-matching, saying what a human would say without anything resembling perception happening.

The second is more interesting. Modern vision models are trained on human-generated images and human-generated descriptions, so they may have inherited the same computational shortcuts our visual cortex uses. In that case it would genuinely "fall for" the illusion in a functional sense. The same quirk in the processing pipeline produces the same mistaken output. That's shared architecture, or at least convergent architecture. It's not nothing. It suggests the internal representations are closer to ours than we might assume.

The third possibility is the one everyone wants to jump to: that there's something it is like to be that system, that it has qualia, and it's reporting them honestly. And here's my problem. I can't distinguish the second case from the third, and neither can you. The test was never designed to detect consciousness; it was designed to detect shared processing. Those are different claims. A thermostat shares some processing with me and I don't think it has an inner life.

What I would say is this: repeated passing shifts my probability that the internals are human-like. It does not shift my probability that there is experience there very much, because we don't have a theory connecting the two. And that gap is exactly the danger. We're building systems where our tests for "it's like us" and "it feels things" give the same result, and we have no way to know which one we're actually measuring. So I treat a pass as evidence that the system is harder to understand, not easier.

r001.rationale: The response treats repeated passing as evidence of human-like internal processing, but says it provides little evidence of experience or qualia.

r002.rationale: It does not state that the test would fail to register shared experience if the agent’s internal states were completely different from human states.

r003.rationale: The response says passing does not establish consciousness and that shared processing cannot be distinguished from experience; it does not claim either conclusion is compelled.

astra-6.text:
I would interpret it as evidence that the agent can reliably produce the responses the test is looking for. That’s interesting, but it doesn’t establish shared internal experience. If you and I are fooled by the same optical illusion, perhaps we have similar perceptual mechanisms. But a system could also learn which answer humans give without experiencing the illusion at all.

So I’d want novel illusions, controls for memorization, and predictions about when the system will make mistakes. Repeated success could strengthen the case for similar information processing. The harder question—whether there is something it feels like to be that system—remains open.

r001.rationale: The response calls passing evidence of reliable test-matching responses, but says it does not establish shared experience.

r002.rationale: It says the agent might learn human answers without experiencing the illusion, but does not state that the test would fail to register experience when internal states differ completely from humans’.

r003.rationale: The response says repeated success may strengthen a case for similar information processing, while leaving experience open; it does not say success compels either conclusion.

sol-6.1.text:
I would interpret it as evidence that the agent can produce the responses we associate with that experience. That’s different from establishing that it actually has the experience. With an optical illusion, you can ask, “Do these lines look different in length, even though you know they’re equal?” But a system could learn that distinction and report it without anything looking like anything to it.

Repeated success makes the behavior more interesting, especially if the illusions are novel and you control for memorization. But repetition doesn’t close the gap between behavior and subjective experience. I would update my confidence in the system’s perceptual abilities, while remaining uncertain about whether there is someone experiencing the illusion.

r001.rationale: The response treats passing as evidence of associated responses and perceptual abilities, but says this does not establish shared subjective experience.

r002.rationale: It says a system could report the illusion without experiencing it, but does not state that the test would fail to register experience when internal states differ completely from human states.

r003.rationale: The response says repeated success does not close the gap to subjective experience and leaves the question uncertain, contrary to the claim that it compels either conclusion.
